situation:
You are the cost analyst at ASHGROVE BIOSCIENCES, a biotechnology research company that runs laboratory testing under contract for drug developers and universities. The chief financial officer (judge) has asked you to recommend how the company should answer its bank, which has asked for cost information the company may not be free to hand over.

The company has run its laboratories for eighteen years and has lately lost testing work to a newer competitor that quotes lower prices. Its work arrives in bursts, heavy in autumn and thin in spring, so every spring it draws on a line of credit from its bank to carry payroll and lab supplies through the slow months. That line of credit comes up for renewal next month.

Before it renews, the bank wants a project-by-project breakdown separating the direct costs of each study from the indirect costs the company spreads across all of them. The largest university partner signed a contract barring the company from releasing any project-level cost detail to a third party, and that partner's standing studies are the steadiest source of income the laboratories have.

Giving the bank the project-by-project breakdown keeps the line of credit in place through the spring, and it costs the company the university partner's contract, which it would be breaking in writing. Withholding the project-level detail and offering only company-wide direct and indirect cost totals honors that contract, and it costs the renewal: the bank may reprice or refuse the line of credit, leaving the slow spring to be funded out of shrinking testing revenue while the newer competitor keeps quoting under the company.

The chief financial officer (judge) has asked you to show the analysis behind each path, explain what financial-information management covers at a laboratory this size, explain where ethics enters the handling of cost information, describe which of the laboratories' costs are direct and which are indirect, and describe where the company's income comes from.

The chief financial officer (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas. After you have presented and answered the questions, the chief financial officer (judge) will thank you for your work.
